prime.problem: A classic database treats disk as home and memory as a cache, so every access pays for buffer-pool machinery and every transaction can stall on a disk read. For OLTP data that mostly fits in RAM, that design wastes most of its time.
prime.fits: Third memory card. It builds on the previous card (disk-era overhead is where the time goes) and on the caching card (two copies to keep in sync); the next card, log-structured memory, is another way to run a store entirely in DRAM.
expect: H-Store: shared-nothing, one thread per partition, stored procedures
anti-caching: evict cold tuples in blocks
prime.goal: Trace a transaction that touches evicted tuples, explain why H-Store never waits on disk, and judge when anti-caching beats a buffer pool or a cache in front.

attend: If RAM is volatile, what does each of the four durability strategies actually keep across a crash?
Why does one thread per partition remove locks and latches, and what kind of transaction does that design make expensive?
Why does a transaction that touches an evicted tuple abort instead of waiting for the disk, and what does the pre-pass buy?
Why must the LRU chain be doubly linked when the touched tuples are hot and sit near the tail?
Why do bigger eviction blocks cost nothing extra on writes but hurt on reads?

must: OLTP databases are mostly under 1 TB → the whole working set fits in RAM → disk is used only for recovery (log, snapshots, replicas) → no query waits on a disk read

Each core owns a partition and runs its transactions one at a time through stored procedures → no locks, latches or client round trips → the overhead the previous card measured disappears (82× TPC-C in 2007)
Data outgrows RAM → evict the coldest tuples in blocks, recorded in an Evicted Table → a tuple lives in exactly one place (RAM or disk), so no sync problem

A transaction meets evicted tuples → a pre-pass records all of them without changing anything → abort, fetch the blocks in the background, merge just those tuples, restart → the single thread never sits on the disk
elevated: The LRU chain is updated on each touch → unlinking needs the predecessor → doubly linked makes it 1 hop instead of ~n from the cold head → sampling only 1% of transactions (aLRU) keeps the cost at 2–7% of throughput
Fetching one tuple brings back its whole block → 1 MB blocks fetch 4× the bytes of 256 KB for one 1,000 B tuple → larger blocks hurt most under high skew
reference: Redis AOF and RDB settings, VoltDB command logging
the 50% hole threshold for compacting blocks

compress.prompt: From memory, draw the life of T2 from the card: in-memory index lookup, pre-pass, abort, fetch, merge, restart, commit, evict. Then in three sentences say why this beats waiting for the disk and what workload breaks it.
checklist: memory is home; disk holds only cold, evicted tuples
one copy of each tuple, tracked by the Evicted Table
the pre-pass finds every evicted tuple before any change, then aborts
fetch runs in the background while other transactions proceed; only needed tuples are merged
low skew or full-table scans defeat it

retrieve.q: Explain the phrase ‘the buffer pool turned inside out’: what is home and what is overflow in each design?
answer: buffer pool: disk is home, memory holds copies of hot pages
anti-caching: memory is home, disk holds evicted cold tuples
so a tuple has exactly one location, and hot data never pays disk-format costs

retrieve.q: Walk through step 5 to step 7 of the card's hand trace: what the pre-pass finds, which blocks are fetched, and what gets evicted at the end.
answer: T2 reads 3, 1, 4: 3 is in memory and is touched; 1 (block 0) and 4 (block 1) are evicted
abort, fetch blocks 0 and 1, merge only tuples 1 and 4
restart and commit [30, 10, 40]; memory now holds 5 tuples, so evict the head [6, 7] as block 2

retrieve.q: Compare anti-caching with MySQL and with MySQL + Memcached on the paper's YCSB runs. Which costs does each alternative pay that anti-caching avoids?
answer: MySQL: disk/memory format conversion and heavyweight locking; anti-caching 9×/18×/10× faster
MySQL + Memcached: two copies to sync and two round trips per miss; 2×/4×/9×, worst on writes
all three slow down as skew drops

retrieve.q: Why can't anti-caching serve a full-table scan well, and where would you run that query instead?
answer: a scan needs every tuple in memory at once
it would fetch every evicted block and abort repeatedly
analytics belong in a column store or a replica built for scans

compare.q: Cache-aside in front of a database and anti-caching both keep hot data in RAM. What is fundamentally different about where the truth lives, and how does each one fail?
answer: cache-aside: the DB is the truth, the cache holds copies
anti-caching: one copy, in RAM or in an evicted block
cache-aside fails with stale sets and herds; anti-caching fails with aborts under low skew and with scans

compare.q: H-Store with anti-caching and RAMCloud both keep data in DRAM. What does each do when memory runs short, and what is the price of that choice?
answer: H-Store evicts cold tuples to disk and aborts transactions that need them
RAMCloud keeps everything in memory and cleans segments to reclaim dead space
anti-caching pays in aborts and fetches; RAMCloud pays u/(1−u) copying and needs headroom

predict.q: Skew drops to uniform: every tuple is equally likely, and the data is 2× RAM, so about half the tuples are evicted. A transaction reads 5 random tuples. Commit first: roughly what fraction of transactions touch no evicted tuple and run without aborting?
predict.answer: Each tuple is in memory with probability about 1/2, so all five are with probability (1/2)<sup>5</sup> ≈ 3.1%. About 97% of transactions abort at least once to fetch blocks, and each fetched block brings in mostly unwanted tuples. That's why the paper finds all systems slow down as skew falls: anti-caching depends on a small hot set.

apply.task: Continue the card's trace. After T2 the chain is [3, 1, 4] and the Evicted Table is {2: block 0, 5: block 1, 6: block 2, 7: block 2}. Run T3, which reads 2 and 6. Write the pre-pass result, the blocks fetched, the commit value and the eviction that follows (cap 4, block size 2). Then say which block is now 100% holes. Check with AntiCache in code/in-memory-db-anticaching.py.
apply.done: Pre-pass finds 2 (block 0) and 6 (block 2), aborts and fetches blocks [0, 2]; T3 commits [20, 60]; memory has 5 tuples, so the head [3, 1] is evicted as block 3; the chain is [4, 2, 6]. Block 0's two tuples (1 and 2) have both been merged back, so it is all holes and due for compaction.
apply.hint: Tuple-merge moves only the needed tuples into memory; their old copies stay in the block as holes.
